docs.title: Title
docs.text: ScreenGrab: Software Bloat and the Generated Alternative

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This short course uses one small utility to show how software bloats, and what generative AI now makes possible when it does. It follows a real case: replacing a paid screen grab tool with a custom app that does only what its one user needs.

docs.title: How a simple tool became a subscription
docs.text:
The story starts with a simple screen grab utility that cost $9 and ran on all of the author's computers. Over the years it gained many more features, and it now requires an annual fee of $30 per computer.

The author has three main computers, so the same job now costs $90 a year, or $450 over five years, compared with the original $9.

This is the core pattern of software bloat. As a rule of thumb, 95% of users use only 5% of the features. Everyone still pays for the rest, including people who never open them.

docs.title: The alternative: generate only what you need
docs.text: Generative AI offers another way out. Instead of paying for a large product or searching for a smaller one, a user can describe the few features they actually use and generate their own tool. The author needed just two: grab a region, and grab a region after a delay, with the image going to the clipboard.

docs.title: How the first version was built
docs.text:
The author gave Claude Code a short request, answered four multiple-choice questions, and later asked for it to be installed with a README. The work moved through a set order: specification, design, code, tests, and installer.

Result at first install Amount App code about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, with no third-party dependencies Tests about 1,370 lines, with 94 automated tests Install and build scripts about 500 lines Specification, design, and README about 1,340 lines Total about 5,200 lines Stage Wall-clock time from first prompt New tokens, including output Output tokens Cache reads Estimated API cost Built and installed about 36 minutes about 500,000 about 206,000 about 3.8 million about $6 First real screen grab about 44 minutes about 573,000 about 238,000 about 6.3 million about $8 Whole session, including hotkey testing about 70 active minutes about 1.15 million about 325,000 about 18.9 million about $14

These costs are estimates. They apply Claude Opus 5.5 API prices of $20 per million output tokens and $0.20 per million cache reads, and treat all other new tokens as cache writes at $5 per million. The session started on the cheaper Sonnet 5.5 and ran on a subscription rather than the API, where the build used about 5% of one five-hour usage window. The figures cover the code only. They exclude generating this textbook, the author's own time, and later maintenance.

docs.title: The results
docs.text:
• The app is installed, and grabs from both the menu and the Control-Shift-4 hotkey have been seen working.
  • At about $6 to build and about $14 for the whole session, the first version cost less than one-sixth of a single year's $90 in fees.
  • The current version is fully open source under the MIT License, and everyone can use it without any fee.
  • The work wasn't flawless. One early hotkey failure was never explained, several acceptance tests still have to be run by hand, and a later fix was needed for Macs with only the Command Line Tools.

docs.title: ScreenGrab — Design
docs.text: Status Draft v0.1 Date 2026-11-01 Implements specification.md

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
ScreenGrab is a menu bar agent written in Swift with AppKit and ScreenCaptureKit. It has no third-party dependencies and builds with the Command Line Tools alone.

A grab has four stages:

  1. Trigger: a global hotkey or a menu item.
  2. Freeze: every display is captured to an in-memory still image. For a delayed grab, this happens when the countdown reaches zero.
  3. Select: an overlay on each display shows that still image, dimmed. The user drags a rectangle.
  4. Output: the rectangle is cropped from the still image, with no second capture, and placed on the clipboard.

Freezing first is the central design decision. It is explained in §2.1.

docs.title: 2.1 Freeze-frame selection
docs.text:
The selector has to show a crosshair and receive the Esc key. It also must not change what ends up in the image. Two small test programs were run on the target machine (macOS 26.6.2) to find out what a background app can do:

Test Result Non-activating panel, NSCursor.crosshair.set() Frontmost app unchanged and panel became key, but the system cursor stayed an arrow (hotspot 5,5) Panel plus NSApp.activate, NSCursor.crosshair.set() System cursor became a crosshair (hotspot 11,11) After that, orderOut and previousApp.activate() Focus returned to the previous app and the arrow cursor came back

So a crosshair requires activating ScreenGrab. Activation has side effects: the previously frontmost window greys out its title bar and traffic lights, and open menus in other apps close. In a live-capture design those changes would appear in the grab.

Capturing before activating removes the conflict:

Concern Live capture on mouse-up Freeze-frame (chosen) Crosshair and Esc Needs activation, which changes the screen Reliable; activation happens after the image is taken Active window title bars Greyed out in the grab Preserved Open menus and hover states Can close before the capture Preserved, which is the main purpose of a delayed grab Own overlay in the image Must be excluded Impossible, because the image predates the overlay What you see vs. what you get Content can change between selecting and capturing Identical pixels Animations and video Keep moving during selection Appear paused (accepted) Memory Small One full frame per display while selecting (about 17 MB per Retina display), freed afterwards Latency Overlay appears at once Overlay waits for the capture (NFR-1 allows 300 ms)

docs.title: 2.2 Other decisions
docs.text: Decision Choice Rationale Capture API SCScreenshotManager.captureImage(contentFilter:configuration:), macOS 14+ Current supported API. CGWindowListCreateImage is no longer available. Global hotkeys Carbon RegisterEventHotKey Needs no Accessibility or Input Monitoring permission (FR-7.2). Registration returned noErr on the target machine in testing. Event taps would need those permissions. Color Always capture in sRGB Tagged sRGB pastes predictably everywhere. Colors outside sRGB clip slightly, which is acceptable for screenshots. Pasteboard formats PNG and LZW-compressed TIFF Some apps prefer one or the other. Package structure Library ScreenGrabKit plus a one-file executable ScreenGrab Lets tests import everything, including views. Tests Swift Testing (import Testing), run through scripts/test.sh The Command Line Tools ship Testing.framework but not XCTest. With these tools alone, and depending on the Swift version, SwiftPM may not find the framework, its macro plugin, or the lib_TestingInterop.dylib it loads at run time, so the script passes all three locations. Swift language mode Swift 5 (swift-tools-version: 5.9) Avoids strict-concurrency friction with AppKit and Carbon callbacks. UI types are still annotated @MainActor. UI construction Programmatic AppKit No Xcode means no storyboards or nibs. Capture sound System Screen Capture.aif, falling back to Pop The file is present on the target machine, but the path isn't a public API, so the fallback is needed.

docs.title: 4.1 Testing seams
docs.text:
GrabCoordinator reaches its collaborators through small protocols, so the state machine can run in tests with no screen, no permission, and no windows:

protocol DisplayCapturing     { func captureAllDisplays() async throws -> [FrozenDisplay] }
protocol PermissionChecking   { func ensureGranted() -> Bool }
protocol CountdownPresenting  { func start(seconds: Int, onFinish: @escaping () -> Void, onCancel: @escaping () -> Void); func stop() }
protocol SelectionPresenting  { func begin(_ frames: [FrozenDisplay], onFinish: @escaping (GrabSelection?) -> Void); func cancel() }
protocol GrabOutputting       { func deliver(_ selection: GrabSelection) async -> GrabOutcome }
protocol GrabFeedback         { func grabSucceeded(); func grabFailed(_ failure: GrabFailure) }

docs.title: 5.1 State machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> idle
    idle --> countingDown: delayed trigger, permission OK
    idle --> freezing: immediate trigger, permission OK
    countingDown --> freezing: countdown reaches zero
    countingDown --> idle: cancel (HUD click, menu, hotkey again)
    freezing --> selecting: frames captured
    freezing --> idle: capture error or cancel
    selecting --> delivering: valid rectangle
    selecting --> idle: Esc, right-click, tiny selection, display change
    delivering --> idle: clipboard written, feedback given

Trigger handling by state (FR-2.10, FR-3.4):

State Grab Region trigger Delayed trigger cancel() idle Starts Starts No effect countingDown Ignored Cancels Cancels freezing Ignored Ignored Cancels; late frames are discarded selecting Ignored Ignored Cancels delivering Ignored Ignored No effect; delivery is nearly complete

docs.text:

sequenceDiagram

    participant GC as GrabCoordinator
    participant HUD as CountdownHUD
    participant CAP as ScreenCapturer
    participant SEL as RegionSelector

docs.title: 6. Coordinate systems and geometry
docs.text:
Screen capture bugs usually come from mixing origins and units. Freeze-frame reduces the problem to one conversion.

Space Origin Unit Used by AppKit global Bottom-left of primary display Points NSScreen.frame, panel placement View local Top-left of the display (views are flipped) Points All selection logic Image Top-left of the frozen image Pixels CGImage.cropping(to:)
  • AppKit global coordinates appear in one place: each panel's frame is set to screen.frame. AppKit handles the placement, and no global math is done by hand.
  • The overlay view fills its display and has isFlipped = true, so a view point is already a top-left-origin, display-local position.
  • Both view and image coordinates have a top-left origin, so no Y flip is needed. Only the scale differs:
scale     = frozenImage.pixelWidth / screen.frame.width
pixelRect = pointRect × scale, rounded to whole pixels, clamped to the image bounds

The scale comes from the actual image rather than backingScaleFactor, so a scaled display mode can't cause a mismatch between what was highlighted and what is cropped. Each FrozenDisplay carries its own scale, which handles mixed-DPI setups (FR-4.3).

Pure functions in SelectionGeometry, all unit-tested:

Function Purpose Requirement selectionRect(from:to:within:) Normalizes a drag in any direction and clamps it to the display FR-2.3, FR-4.1 pixelRect(forPointRect:scale:imagePixelSize:) Point-to-pixel conversion with rounding and clamping FR-4.3, NFR-6 isAccidental(pixelRect:) True when either dimension is under 4 pixels FR-2.6 labelOrigin(pointer:labelSize:bounds:) Places the label near the pointer, keeping it on screen FR-4.4

docs.title: 7.1 ScreenCapturer
docs.text:
For each NSScreen, the SCDisplay is matched by CGDirectDisplayID (from the screen's NSScreenNumber), then captured with:

Setting Value Why Filter SCContentFilter(display:excludingApplications:[self],exceptingWindows:[]) Keeps ScreenGrab's Preferences window and the closing HUD out of the frame (FR-2.7) width, height Display points × backingScaleFactor Native pixels (A2, NFR-6) captureResolution .best No downsampling showsCursor false A1 colorSpaceName sRGB §2.2

SCShareableContent is fetched fresh for each grab, so display changes are always reflected. Frames are captured concurrently.

Excluding the whole app also removes ScreenGrab's own menu bar icon from grabs of the menu bar. This is a harmless side effect of FR-2.7.

When a grab starts from the menu rather than a hotkey, the coordinator waits about 100 ms first so the closing menu isn't in the frame.

docs.title: 7.2 RegionSelector and overlay views
docs.text:
Panel: one NSPanel per display, borderless and .nonactivatingPanel, with canBecomeKey = true, level = .screenSaver (above the menu bar and Dock), and collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .stationary, .ignoresCycle].

Start sequence:

  1. Record NSWorkspace.shared.frontmostApplication.
  2. Order all panels front; the panel under the pointer becomes key.
  3. Call NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps: true). This is the call tested in §2.1. It is deprecated from macOS 14 but works; the newer activate() is cooperative and could be refused.
  4. Register .crosshair as the cursor rect across each overlay, and set it again when the app's activation completes, because the pointer may not be moving at that moment.

View hierarchy (two layers, so a drag never repaints the image):

  • FrozenImageView draws the still image once.
  • SelectionOverlayView is on top and transparent. It draws the dimming (an even-odd fill with the selection as a hole), the border, and the size label, invalidating only the changed area. It receives all mouse and keyboard events.

Input:

Event Action acceptsFirstMouse Returns true, so the first click starts the drag mouseDown, mouseDragged Updates the selection through selectionRect. AppKit keeps sending drags to the window that got the mouse-down, which is what confines a selection to one display (FR-4.1) mouseUp Finishes, or cancels if isAccidental rightMouseDown, Esc (keyCode 53) Cancels mouseMoved Updates the position label before a drag starts

Teardown (finish(), single-shot, on every path): order out all panels, release frames, reactivate the previous app unless it is ScreenGrab itself (FR-2.12, FR-4.6), and call the completion handler once.

docs.title: 7.3 CountdownHUD
docs.text:
A borderless, .nonactivatingPanel NSPanel at .screenSaver level. It can't become key and is shown with orderFrontRegardless(), so it never takes focus (FR-3.3). It sits near the top of the display containing the pointer.

  • The timer runs in .common run loop mode so it keeps ticking while the status menu is open. Without this, the Cancel Grab item would freeze the countdown.
  • The display is computed from a fixed deadline, ceil(deadline − now), to avoid drift.
  • acceptsFirstMouse plus mouseDown provide click-to-cancel.

docs.title: 7.4 GrabOutput and ImageEncoder
docs.text:
deliver(selection):
    pixelRect = SelectionGeometry.pixelRect(...)
    cropped   = frame.image.cropping(to: pixelRect)
    encoded   = ImageEncoder.encode(cropped, scale)   // off the main thread
    write clipboard                                   // on the main thread
    if settings.saveToFolder: save PNG
  • Encoding uses CGImageDestination with kCGImagePropertyDPIWidth and kCGImagePropertyDPIHeight set to 72 × scale. That metadata is what makes a 2× image paste at its on-screen size (FR-5.2).
  • Clipboard: clearContents(), then .png and .tiff data. The pasteboard is an injected parameter, so tests use a private named pasteboard and never touch the user's real clipboard.
  • Saving runs after the clipboard write. A save failure is reported but doesn't undo the copy (FR-5.6). The result is a GrabOutcome that names any failure.
  • FileNaming uses a fixed POSIX-locale date formatter and an injected "exists" check.

docs.title: 7.5 Hotkeys
docs.text:
HotKeyCombo is Codable and stores a virtual key code and Carbon modifier mask. It provides validation (FR-7.3), a display string such as ⌃⇧4, and the menu key equivalent. Key names come from a table of ANSI keys and function keys, so labels assume a US layout.

HotKeyCenter installs one Carbon event handler and maps EventHotKeyID to an action. Shortcuts are registered with kEventHotKeyExclusive, because without it a shortcut another app owns may not be reported as a conflict. A failure such as eventHotKeyExistsErr (-9878) feeds the warning in FR-7.5. Testing confirmed that a second process trying to take a registered shortcut gets this error.

While a ShortcutRecorderButton is recording, all hotkeys are suspended so the keys being recorded don't start a grab.

docs.title: 7.6 Settings and Preferences
docs.text:
AppSettings wraps UserDefaults, clamps delay values to 1–60, and fires an onChange callback that re-registers hotkeys and refreshes the menu. Preferences apply immediately.

The window is an NSGridView laid out per spec §8.4. Accessory apps have no visible main menu, so a hidden NSApp.mainMenu supplies ⌘W and the standard Edit commands; without it those key equivalents wouldn't work in the custom delay field.

Opening the app while it's already running shows Preferences (FR-6.7). This gives a way in if the menu bar icon is hidden behind the notch.

docs.title: 7.7 Screen Recording permission
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Grab triggered] --> B{CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess}
    B -- granted --> C[Continue grab]
    B -- not granted --> D[CGRequestScreenCaptureAccess]
    D --> E[Alert with Open System Settings]
    E --> F[Grab aborted]

The check runs before the countdown, so the user doesn't wait through a delay only to see an error. If a capture later fails with SCStreamError.userDeclined, the same alert is shown. Nothing is ever pasted from a failed capture (FR-8.4).

The settings pane URL is x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_ScreenCapture.

docs.title: 7.8 Status menu and feedback
docs.text:
NSMenuDelegate.menuNeedsUpdate rebuilds dynamic state: the delay in the title, the checkmark in the Delay submenu, shortcut display, and Cancel Grab visibility.

On success, the icon switches from camera.viewfinder to checkmark.circle for one second, using template images so it follows light and dark menu bars.

docs.title: 8. Concurrency model
docs.text:
• All UI types and GrabCoordinator are @MainActor.
  • Carbon hotkey callbacks arrive on the main thread through the main run loop.
  • Capture is async and suspends without blocking the UI. PNG and TIFF encoding run in a detached task.
  • Stale results: each grab gets a generation number. When captureAllDisplays() returns, its result is discarded if the generation has moved on, for example after a cancel during freezing.

docs.title: 10.1 Automated (swift test)
docs.text:
Automated tests need no permissions, don't touch the real clipboard, and put nothing on the visible screen. Most views render without being shown. One test orders a window far off-screen, because only a window that is ordered in has real layer backing stores.

Area What is verified SelectionGeometry Drags in all four directions; clamping; 1×, 2×, and fractional scales; rounding; accidental threshold; label flipping at edges Crop accuracy A synthetic image with known pixel colors is cropped through the real functions, and the exact output pixels are checked, including at 2× ImageEncoder PNG and TIFF decode to the expected size; DPI metadata is 144 at 2× Clipboard Round trip through a private named pasteboard; both types present; previous contents replaced FileNaming, save Format, collision suffixes, folder creation, unwritable-folder error HotKeyCombo Validation rules, duplicates, display strings, Codable round trip HotKeyCenter Registration, conflict reporting, suspend and resume; a Carbon hotkey event built by hand reaches the handler with the right action (this tests everything after the key press itself) AppSettings Defaults, clamping, persistence (with an in-memory UserDefaults subclass, because a real suite leaves a plist behind on every run) GrabCoordinator Every cell of the §5.1 table using fakes, including stale frames after a cancel and repeated triggers SelectionOverlayView Synthesized mouse and key events produce the right selection or cancel; the view hierarchy renders off-screen to a bitmap, with pixels checked for dimming, the undimmed hole, and correct orientation; repeated partial redraws don't accumulate dimming in the layer's backing store

docs.title: 10.2 Smoke test (no permission needed)
docs.text:
These checks run against the installed app, and none of them trigger a permission prompt:

Check How Runs with no Dock icon lsappinfo info ScreenGrab reports type="UIElement" A second launch exits Run the binary directly; the first process keeps its ID Holds its hotkeys A second process making an exclusive RegisterEventHotKey call for ⌃⇧4 gets -9878 with ScreenGrab running, and succeeds with it stopped. A non-exclusive call succeeds either way, so it can't detect a conflict. Menu bar icon exists A probe status item's x position shifts by the width of one item when ScreenGrab is running compared with stopped Idle cost ps reports CPU and resident memory

The menu bar icon needs this indirect check. On macOS 26, CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo doesn't list third-party status items, even for the process that owns them.

A real key press can't be simulated from a process without Accessibility access, so hotkey delivery has to be tried by hand. The unified log then shows how a grab started: a menu grab logs perform action for menu item just before its capture, and a hotkey grab doesn't. Scripts should call /usr/bin/log by its full path, because plain log is a zsh builtin in non-interactive shells. /etc/zshrc disables that builtin only for interactive ones.

docs.title: 10.3 Manual acceptance
docs.text: Real capture needs the Screen Recording grant, and real pointer input needs a person, so the acceptance tests in spec §10 are run by hand. These cover what automation can't reach: actual ScreenCaptureKit output, on-screen overlay behavior, the live crosshair, and pasting into real applications.

docs.title: 11. Build, packaging, and signing
docs.text:
src/scripts/build-app.sh:

  1. swift build -c release --package-path src. With UNIVERSAL=1, each architecture is built in its own scratch folder and the results are combined with lipo.
  2. Assembles dist/ScreenGrab.app/Contents/{MacOS/ScreenGrab, Info.plist, PkgInfo} in a staging folder.
  3. codesign --force --sign "${SIGN_IDENTITY:--}", then verifies the signature.
  4. Replaces any previous build only once the new one is complete.

src/install.sh wraps this for installation. Its order is chosen so that the installed app keeps working if anything goes wrong:

  1. Checks the OS, the build tools, and the destination. It refuses to replace an app with a different bundle identifier, or to run as root.
  2. Runs the tests, then builds. A failure here leaves the installed app untouched and still running.
  3. Copies the build beside the target and verifies the copy.
  4. Stops the running app, moves the old version aside, and moves the new one into place. An exit trap restores the old version if the swap doesn't complete.
  5. Removes the old version, registers the new one with LaunchServices, and opens it.

The script is written for Bash 3.2, the version macOS ships.

Info.plist key values:

Key Value CFBundleIdentifier com.dmccreary.screengrab LSUIElement true (no Dock icon) LSMinimumSystemVersion 14.0

Signing and the Screen Recording grant: macOS identifies an ad-hoc signed app by its code hash, which changes on every rebuild, so each rebuild needs the permission granted again. Setting SIGN_IDENTITY to a stable self-signed certificate avoids this. src/README.md gives the Keychain Access steps. Because this changes the user's keychain, the scripts never create a certificate on their own.

docs.title: ScreenGrab — Product Specification
docs.text: Status Draft v0.1 Date 2026-11-01 Requirements owner Dan McCreary Platform macOS only (14 Sonoma or later) Related documents design.md

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
ScreenGrab is a small, free, single-purpose macOS utility that replaces the one part of Snagit that is actually used: grabbing a rectangular region of the screen and putting the image on the clipboard. Snagit moved to an annual license; the owner only uses it for screen grabs, so paying for the editor, library, video capture, and sharing features is not worthwhile.

The working name is ScreenGrab.

docs.title: 2.1 Goals
docs.text:
1. Capture a user-selected rectangular region of any display with a single gesture (hotkey → drag).
  2. Capture the same way after a user-configurable countdown, so transient content (open menus, hover states, tooltips) can be arranged first.
  3. Put the resulting image on the clipboard, ready to paste, by default and without any extra step.
  4. Be tiny, fast, quiet, and invisible until needed (menu bar only).
  5. Be buildable from source on the owner's machine with the tools already installed (Swift Command Line Tools; no full Xcode required).

docs.title: 2.2 Non-goals (v1)
docs.text:
• No image editor, annotation, markup, or effects.
  • No full-screen, window, scrolling, or video capture modes.
  • No capture library / history, tagging, or cloud sharing.
  • No OCR, text grab, or QR scanning.
  • No compatibility with Snagit file formats (.snagx) or its presets.
  • No App Store distribution, notarization, auto-update, or telemetry.

See §12 for the list of ideas deferred beyond v1.

docs.title: 3. Users and context
docs.text:
Single user: the owner. Typical use is capturing parts of web pages, apps, and diagrams to paste into documents, slide decks, chat, and the figures of MkDocs-based intelligent textbooks. Because the user pastes into many different applications, the clipboard image must work broadly (Keynote, Pages, Word, Google Docs, Slack, browsers, Preview "New from Clipboard", etc.).

The user's display is a Retina laptop panel (2560×1664 native); external displays and mixed-DPI setups are possible.

docs.title: 4. Decisions made during requirements clarification
docs.text:
The following answers were given by the owner and are binding for v1.

# Question Decision D1 Technology Native Swift (Swift Package, AppKit, ScreenCaptureKit) D2 How a grab is triggered Menu bar app + global hotkeys (menu items as a fallback) D3 How the delay works Presets + custom value. A visible countdown runs first; when it finishes the region selector appears D4 Output Clipboard only by default. An optional preference also saves a PNG to a folder (off by default) D5 Interface complexity Keep it simple; only Grab Region and Grab Region with Delay exist in v1

One further decision came out of testing during design, and it supports D3 rather than changing it:

# Topic Decision D6 Selection model Freeze-frame. Every display is captured the instant the selector starts, and the overlay shows that still image. Testing on macOS 26 showed that a background app can't display a crosshair, and activating the app changes what is on screen. Capturing first means those changes never reach the image. See design §2.1.

docs.title: 4.1 Assumptions made by the specification author
docs.text:
These were not explicitly discussed; each is a sensible default and is easy to change. Please veto any that are wrong.

# Assumption A1 The mouse cursor is not included in captured images. A2 Images are captured at the display's native pixel resolution (2× on Retina) and are never downscaled. A3 A selection can't span multiple displays; it is confined to the display where the drag began. A4 A short confirmation sound plays on success (can be turned off). A5 Default hotkeys are ⌃⇧4 (Grab Region) and ⌃⇧5 (Grab Region with Delay). Both are user-changeable. A6 Default delay is 5 seconds; presets are 3, 5, 10, 15 s; custom range is 1–60 s. A7 The optional save folder defaults to ~/Pictures/ScreenGrab. A8 Local-only distribution: built from source, ad-hoc or self-signed, not notarized.

docs.title: 5. Platform and constraints
docs.text: Item Requirement OS macOS 14.0 (Sonoma) or later. Developed and tested on macOS 26. CPU Apple Silicon (primary). Intel supported via an optional universal build. Language / UI Swift 5 language mode (toolchain Swift 6.x), AppKit Capture API ScreenCaptureKit (SCScreenshotManager). CGWindowListCreateImage is unavailable on current macOS and is not used. Build tooling Swift Package Manager and the Xcode Command Line Tools only. No Xcode.app dependency. Third-party dependencies None. Sandboxing Not sandboxed (personal tool, not App Store). Network None. The app makes no network connections.

docs.title: 6. Functional requirements
docs.text: Requirement IDs are stable and referenced from the acceptance tests in §10.

docs.title: 6.1 Application presence (menu bar agent)
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-1.1 The app runs as a menu bar agent: no Dock icon, no app-switcher entry, no main window. FR-1.2 A status item (icon) appears in the menu bar while the app runs. Clicking it opens the menu described in §8.1. FR-1.3 Only one instance may run. Launching a second instance exits immediately. FR-1.4 Quit is available from the menu (⌘Q while the menu is open). FR-1.5 Launching the app shows no windows or alerts. A permission request occurs only when the first grab is attempted (see FR-8.x).

docs.title: 6.2 Grab Region
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-2.1 Grab Region can be started from the menu item or its global hotkey (default ⌃⇧4), regardless of which application is frontmost. FR-2.2 On start, every connected display is captured immediately (freeze-frame). An overlay covers each display, including displays showing full-screen apps, and shows that still image dimmed. The system cursor becomes a crosshair. FR-2.3 The user presses the mouse button, drags to define a rectangle in any direction, and releases. Release performs the capture immediately (no confirm step). FR-2.4 While dragging, the selected area is shown un-dimmed with a thin border, and a live label shows the selection size in pixels (e.g. 640 × 480). FR-2.5 Esc or a right-click cancels the grab. Cancelling leaves the clipboard untouched and produces no sound. FR-2.6 A selection smaller than 4 × 4 pixels (an accidental click) is treated as a cancel. FR-2.7 ScreenGrab's own overlay, labels, and countdown HUD never appear in the captured image. FR-2.8 The captured image replaces the clipboard contents (see §6.5). FR-2.9 On success the user gets feedback per §6.9. FR-2.10 Starting a grab while another grab or countdown is already in progress is ignored (except the cancel behavior in FR-3.4). FR-2.11 The grabbed image shows the screen exactly as it was when the selector started. Open menus, hover states, tooltips, and active window title bars are preserved, even if the real windows change underneath the overlay. FR-2.12 When a grab ends by any path, keyboard focus returns to the application that was frontmost before the selector appeared.

docs.title: 6.3 Grab Region with Delay
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-3.1 Grab Region with Delay can be started from the menu item or its global hotkey (default ⌃⇧5). FR-3.2 The delay is a whole number of seconds, 1–60, default 5. Presets of 3, 5, 10, 15 are offered; a custom value may be entered. The current value is shown in the menu item title, e.g. Grab Region with Delay (5 s). FR-3.3 On start, a countdown HUD appears showing the remaining seconds, updating every second. The HUD must not take keyboard focus or activate ScreenGrab, so the application and any open menu or hover state the user is preparing is left undisturbed. FR-3.4 The countdown can be cancelled by (a) clicking the HUD, (b) choosing Cancel Grab in the menu bar menu (the item is visible only while a countdown or selection is active), or (c) pressing the Grab-with-Delay hotkey again. FR-3.5 When the countdown reaches zero the HUD closes, the screen is frozen at that instant, and the same region selector as FR-2.2 – FR-2.8 appears. Anything arranged during the countdown, such as an open menu, is in the frozen image and can be selected. FR-3.6 The delay in effect when the countdown starts is used for that grab; changing it mid-countdown affects only later grabs.

docs.title: 6.4 Region selection behavior
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-4.1 The selection is confined to the display on which the mouse button went down; dragging beyond that display's edge clamps to the edge. FR-4.2 The overlay must appear above normal windows, the menu bar, and the Dock, and on whichever Space is active. FR-4.3 The overlay must work on mixed-DPI setups (e.g. Retina laptop panel plus a non-Retina external monitor); the captured area exactly matches what was highlighted. FR-4.4 The size label is placed near the pointer and stays fully on screen (flipping side near edges). FR-4.5 Pointer coordinates and the label are updated at interactive frame rates (no visible lag when dragging). FR-4.6 The overlay is dismissed on every exit path (success, cancel, error) and the cursor is restored.

docs.title: 6.5 Output
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-5.1 Default behavior: the captured image is written to the general pasteboard as PNG and TIFF representations so it pastes into the widest range of applications. FR-5.2 Retina fidelity: the image keeps native pixels (2× on Retina). Its size/DPI metadata is set so that the pasted image appears at the same on-screen size as the captured region (72 × scale DPI). FR-5.3 The app writes nothing to disk unless the optional save preference is enabled (no temp files, no logs containing image data). FR-5.4 Optional save (off by default): when enabled, the same image is also saved as a PNG in the chosen folder, in addition to the clipboard. FR-5.5 Saved filename: ScreenGrab yyyy-MM-dd 'at' HH.mm.ss.png (local time, mirrors macOS's own screenshot naming). If the name already exists, a numeric suffix is added: … (2).png. FR-5.6 The save folder is created if it doesn't exist. If saving fails (permissions, disk full), the clipboard copy still succeeds and the user is shown an error describing the save failure.

docs.title: 6.6 Preferences
docs.text:
A single small Preferences window, opened from the menu (⌘, ) — see the layout in §8.4. Changes apply immediately (no OK/Apply).

ID Requirement FR-6.1 Delay: presets 3 / 5 / 10 / 15 s and Custom… with a numeric field (1–60). FR-6.2 Hotkeys: one recorder control for each of the two actions, each with a reset to default affordance. FR-6.3 Play sound on successful grab (default on). FR-6.4 Also save to folder checkbox (default off) with a Choose… button and the current path displayed. FR-6.5 Preferences persist across launches (user defaults). FR-6.6 A quick Delay submenu in the menu bar menu offers the presets and checks the current one, so the delay can be changed without opening Preferences. FR-6.7 Opening the app while it's already running shows Preferences, which gives a way in if the menu bar icon is hidden behind the notch.

docs.title: 6.7 Global hotkeys
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-7.1 Hotkeys work while any application is frontmost and while ScreenGrab is not the active app. FR-7.2 Registering hotkeys must not require Accessibility or Input Monitoring permission. FR-7.3 A hotkey must include at least one of ⌃ ⌥ ⌘ (a bare key or ⇧-only combination is rejected by the recorder). FR-7.4 The two actions can't be assigned the same shortcut. FR-7.5 If the OS refuses a registration because another app already owns the shortcut, the Preferences window shows a warning next to that control and the menu item remains usable. FR-7.6 The assigned shortcuts are displayed next to the menu items.

docs.title: 6.8 Permissions
docs.text:
macOS requires Screen & System Audio Recording permission to capture the screen.

ID Requirement FR-8.1 Each grab checks permission before doing anything else (for a delayed grab, before the countdown). If permission is missing, the app asks macOS to show its system prompt; macOS itself limits how often that prompt appears. FR-8.2 If permission is missing, the grab is aborted and the user sees an alert explaining what is needed, with a button that opens System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording. FR-8.3 The alert states that the app may need to be quit and reopened after the permission is granted. FR-8.4 A grab never produces a silently blank or wallpaper-only image because of missing permission.

docs.title: 6.9 Feedback and errors
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-9.1 Success is signalled by (a) the menu bar icon switching to a checkmark for about one second, and (b) a short system sound, unless sound is turned off. FR-9.2 Cancel is silent and leaves no visible trace. FR-9.3 Errors are shown in a standard alert with a plain-language message. Covered cases: missing permission, no display found, capture failure, clipboard write failure, save failure. FR-9.4 The overlay and HUD are always torn down, even when an error occurs. FR-9.5 If a display is connected or disconnected mid-grab, the grab is cancelled cleanly without a crash.

docs.title: 6.10 Installation
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-10.1 src/install.sh tests, builds, signs, and installs the app with one command, then opens it. FR-10.2 The default destination is /Applications, falling back to ~/Applications if that isn't writable. A destination can also be chosen. FR-10.3 A failed test or build leaves any installed copy untouched. If replacing the installed copy fails, the previous version is restored. FR-10.4 The installer refuses to replace or remove an app with a different bundle identifier that happens to be named ScreenGrab.app. FR-10.5 The installer checks its prerequisites first and gives a specific instruction for anything missing. It refuses to run as root. FR-10.6 The installer can uninstall the app, optionally deleting its preferences, and can clear the app's Screen Recording entry. FR-10.7 src/README.md documents installation, permissions, usage, troubleshooting, and development.

docs.title: 7. Non-functional requirements
docs.text: ID Category Requirement NFR-1 Responsiveness Overlay visible within 300 ms of the hotkey (excluding countdown). This includes capturing the frozen frames. NFR-2 Capture speed Release-to-clipboard within 300 ms for regions up to ~1 megapixel and within 1 s for a full Retina screen. NFR-3 Idle cost ~0 % CPU while idle; resident memory under 50 MB idle. Frozen frames are released as soon as a grab ends. NFR-4 Privacy No network access, no analytics, no persistence of image data unless FR-5.4 is enabled. Preferences contain no image data. NFR-5 Reliability No crash on cancel, rapid repeated hotkeys, display changes, or empty clipboard states. NFR-6 Quality of image Pixel-exact capture: output pixel size equals selection size × display scale; no resampling blur. NFR-7 Footprint Source of about 2,000 lines of Swift, excluding tests; no third-party packages. NFR-8 Maintainability Pure logic (geometry conversion, file naming, delay clamping, hotkey validation) is separated from UI and unit-tested. NFR-9 Accessibility Menu items and Preferences controls have accessibility labels; every grab can be cancelled from the keyboard (Esc). NFR-10 Buildability src/scripts/build-app.sh produces a runnable ScreenGrab.app on a Mac that has only the Command Line Tools.

docs.title: 11. Risks and known operating-system behavior
docs.text: ID Risk / behavior Mitigation R1 macOS ties the Screen Recording grant to the app's code signature. An ad-hoc signed app gets a new identity whenever its code changes, so the permission must be re-granted after such a rebuild. The scripts accept a SIGN_IDENTITY so a stable self-signed certificate can be used, as documented in src/README.md. The installer warns when the signature has changed. Rebuilds are rare for personal use. R2 Since macOS 15, the system periodically asks the user to re-confirm Screen Recording access for apps that capture the screen. Out of the app's control; documented. R3 The selector has to activate ScreenGrab to show a crosshair, which closes other apps' open menus and greys their title bars. Freeze-frame: the image is captured before activation, so none of this appears in grabs. The remaining effect is that a menu open when the selector starts is closed once the grab ends, including a cancelled one. R4 The chosen shortcuts may collide with other apps. Configurable hotkeys; collision warning (FR-7.5). R5 Content protected by DRM (some video players, Apple TV) captures as black. OS behavior; documented, no workaround. R6 Mixed-DPI coordinate conversion bugs (top-left vs bottom-left origins, points vs pixels). Single tested conversion function; see design §6. R7 Screen capture uses a macOS API that Apple continues to evolve. Isolated behind one ScreenCapturer type. R8 Because the screen is frozen, video and animations appear paused during selection. Intended: the pixels selected are exactly the pixels copied.

docs.title: 12. Out of scope and future ideas
docs.text:
Intentionally not part of v1, in rough priority order if the app grows:

  1. Launch at login.
  2. Hold Space while dragging to reposition the selection; arrow-key nudging.
  3. Pixel magnifier loupe near the cursor for precise edges.
  4. Optional include cursor setting.
  5. Window-snap capture (hover a window to highlight and click to capture it).
  6. Small floating thumbnail after capture with Save As….
  7. Full-screen capture, scrolling capture, delayed full-screen capture.
  8. Basic annotation (arrows, boxes, callouts) — the only Snagit feature likely worth a future investment for documentation work.
  9. Notarized, universal binary distribution.

docs.text: This textbook is organized into 15 chapters covering 206 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat - Defines software, features, versions, and release cycles, then shows how bloat, feature creep, and growing resource footprints arise, contrasted with the single-purpose utility.
  2. Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule - Examines how people actually use software, covering power and casual users, the long tail of features, interface complexity, and the roadmap pressures that keep adding features.
  3. Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives - Compares one-time licenses with subscriptions, starting from copyright, and explains how recurring revenue, switching costs, and lock-in change what vendors choose to build and charge.
  4. Total Cost of Ownership - Teaches readers to calculate per-computer and multi-year costs, break-even points, and the hidden maintenance, learning, and opportunity costs behind a software choice.
  5. Generative AI and Coding Agents - Introduces generative AI, source code, and coding agents such as Claude Code, covering prompts, sessions, permissions, human review, hallucination, and overconfident reporting.
  6. Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software - Frames buy, subscribe, and generate as three options, and weighs disposable and long-lived personal software against the risks and support duties of owning a tool.
  7. Requirements and Minimal Specifications - Moves from user needs to functional requirements, non-goals, and acceptance criteria, showing how a specification that leaves features out defines ScreenGrab's region, delay, and clipboard scope.
  8. Software Design and Platform Constraints - Covers design decisions, trade-offs, prototypes, and zero-dependency design, then applies them to ScreenGrab's menu bar app, global hotkey, screen recording permission, and freeze-frame selection.
  9. Generating, Building, and Installing the Code - Follows generation through compiling, build and installer scripts, code signing, and Git, and closes by assembling the complete ScreenGrab case study.
  10. Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing - Explains input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens, along with context windows, cache expiration, pricing, and how model tiers affect selection.
  11. Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost - Applies token pricing to real sessions, separating wall-clock from active time and breaking the $6 build and $14 session into their cost drivers and assumptions.
  12. Software Testing: Automated and Manual - Introduces verification, unit and integration tests, isolation, stubs, and simulated input, then the manual, acceptance, and smoke tests that automation cannot replace.
  13. Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans - Works through reproduction, root cause analysis, and unexplained failures, then teaches evidence-based reporting and verification plans that separate automated tests from checks a person must run.
  14. Maintenance and Open Source Sharing - Covers technical debt, operating system and toolchain changes, and patch releases, then open source licensing, public repositories, forks, pull requests, and long-term stewardship.
  15. The Final Decision and the Capstone Project - Brings the course together with decision criteria, a decision matrix, and cost per feature used, leading to the capstone: build a replacement tool and publish a cost comparison.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Read the chapters in order the first time through. The sequence follows the book's argument, from how software bloats, to what it costs, to generating, measuring, verifying, and maintaining a replacement, and every concept appears only after the concepts it depends on. Chapter 15 draws on nearly everything before it, so if you plan to complete the capstone, start thinking early about which paid tool you want to replace.

docs.title: Learning Graph for ScreenGrab: Software Bloat and the Generated Alternative
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.
